fewer people would be willing to consent to newborn screening using whole-genome or exon sequencing than to current newborn screening.

integrating whole-genome or whole-exome sequencing (WG or ES) into newborn screening (NRS) might reduce participation, challenge the moral authority of NRS programs and require a shift in the public perception of the parental responsibility to participate, which may have implications for public health.

the ethical implications of integrating genome-wide sequencing into newborn screening, a public health programme that is based upon the moral obligation of parents to participate in screening.
the public’s attitudes regarding the integration of whole genome sequencing in newborn screening.
the public’s willingness to participate in universal screening for rare diseases using WG/ES.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the public is willing to participate in newborn screening using current technology, but not as willing to participate in the same newborn screening using whole genome sequencing.
the public is not ready to accept whole genome sequencing as a part of NBS.
the public is willing to participate in newborn screening but is less willing to participate in whole-genome sequencing.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

there are significant differences in the public’s views on the use of genome sequencing in newborn screening compared with current technologies, with fewer respondents willing to participate in genome sequencing-based newborn screening, and perceiving a parental responsibility to do so.

public support for newborn screening is contingent on the type of screening used, and integrating whole-genome or whole-exome sequencing into newborn screening may reduce public support for participation in the programme.

public views on the use of genome sequencing in newborn screening are mixed.
